message.content:
The answer depends on the definition of finite expectation used in the setting.
In standard probability theory, a random variable has finite expectation only when its absolute value has finite expectation.
That condition is called integrability.
For a discrete variable, integrability means that the sum of absolute values of the outcomes weighted by their probabilities is finite.
If X is integrable, both the positive part and the negative part of X have finite expectations.
The same holds for Y.
Then the triangle inequality gives a direct bound on the absolute value of X plus Y.
Specifically, the absolute value of X plus Y is at most the sum of the absolute values of X and Y.
Therefore the absolute value of X plus Y has finite expectation.
This proves that X plus Y is integrable.
Hence its ordinary expectation exists and is finite.
Moreover, the expectation of X plus Y equals the sum of the expectations of X and Y.
So under the usual definition, no such discrete pair exists.
A different story appears if one uses a weaker and nonstandard notion of finite expectation.
Some authors informally treat a conditionally convergent series as a finite expectation for a discrete variable.
In that weaker sense, a variable can have a finite signed sum while its absolute sum diverges.
Linearity can then fail because the relevant series are not absolutely convergent.
One can arrange probabilities so that X alone cancels enough to give a finite signed sum.
One can arrange the same for Y.
If the joint distribution is chosen badly for the sum, the positive and negative parts of X plus Y can both diverge.
In that nonstandard setting, the expectation of X plus Y may be undefined or infinite.
Thus the answer is yes for conditional series and no for Lebesgue integrability.
Under the standard definition, a finite discrete expectation means the positive and negative parts have finite sums, so X and Y are integrable and their sum is integrable, and no clear path exists beneath the standard integrability requirement.
